extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of Catholic theology (doctrine of grace, predestination, free will)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from a scholarly/theological work summarizing doctrinal positions, canonical pronouncements, and scholastic arguments about grace, free will, vocation, election, and predestination. Intended as a reference for theological study and polemical comparison of Thomist, Molinist, Augustinian, and other views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election not based on foreseen merits
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Deus ordinate vult... ergo prius vult gloriam quam merita, et consequenter electio ad gloriam non potest esse ex praevisione meritorum.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomist formulation (Clypeus Thomist.) arguing that God wills the end (glory) prior to the means (merits), therefore election to glory cannot be grounded in foreseen human merits; cited as a central Thomist argument against the view that foreseen merits determine election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of ‘sufficient grace’
rubrics_metrics.description: In gratia sufficiente totum id continetur quod ad potentiam bene operandi exigitur, non autem id quod ulterius requiritur ad actum; sufficient grace supplies what is required for power but not necessarily for the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with scholastic nuance: sufficient grace confers the potency to do the good (if the will cooperates), and lack of actual good action arises from the defect of will rather than insufficiency of the grace itself (Panoplia; Prael. Theol.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of ‘efficacious grace’
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficacious (efficax) grace is understood as a divine motion that, by virtue of God’s power and decree, infallibly tends to produce the intended supernatural effect in the creature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomist account treats efficacious grace as intrinsically effective (often called a ‘praemotio physica’), while debates with Molinists/Congruists center on whether efficaciousness depends on divine premotion or on foreseen human cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praemotio physica (divine physical premotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Thomist notion that the divine motion given to a created will is ‘physical’ in that it is intrinsic, efficacious, and not dependent on created consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain how God’s causality can determine a will’s actual motion without denying true created liberty; scholarly references (Gonet, Nazarius, Alvarez) and objections/counterarguments are summarized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free will cooperates with grace (Tridentine prohibition of denying cooperation)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is anathema to assert that the human free will, when moved by God, does not cooperate at all in assenting and yet cannot dissent — i.e., to reduce the will to a passive, inert thing utterly without cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council of Trent canons (Sess. VI, can. 4 & related) condemn formulations that eliminate human cooperation; theological positions must preserve that grace aids and moves but does not render the will merely passive or unable to dissent in moral terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith as the beginning/foundation of justification
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Fides est humanae salutis initium, fundamentum et radix omnis iustificationis.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tridentine teaching (Sess. VI, cap. 8) that faith — conceived through hearing and moved by divine grace — is the starting point of justification; the text also treats faith as a gift of God (see Sess. III, cap. 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Justifying faith is not mere trust in divine mercy
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Si quis dixerit, fidem iustificantem nihil aliud esse quam fiduciam divinae misericordiae... anathema sit.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council of Trent (Sess. VI, can. 12) rejects a reduced notion of justifying faith as mere trust; doctrinal formulations of faith must acknowledge its fuller content (assent to revealed truth, infused virtue, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation for justification requires divinely excited faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Those are disposed to justification when, excited by divine grace and aided, they freely move toward God, believing what is revealed and promised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tridentine cap. 6 emphasizes that divine grace excites and aids the human response; justification presupposes both the divine excitation and the free movement of the believer in response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anathema on making justification exclusive to the predestined
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Si quis iustificationis gratiam nonnisi praedestinatis ad vitam contingere dixerit... anathema sit.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council of Trent (Sess. VI, can. 17, Denzinger-Bannwart n. 827) condemns teaching that only the predestined receive justifying grace; the universal call and offer of grace must be maintained against formulations that restrict it to a preselected elect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Molinist account: prevenient aid depends on free cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: Molina: auxiliis praevenientis atque adiuvantis gratiae pendere a libero consensu et cooperatione liberi arbitrii nostri; prevenient aid leaves the free consent and cooperation to the creature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Molinist position (Molina, Concordia) argues that prevenient aid inclines but does not force the will; discussions contrast this with Thomist claims and address cases of equal interior aid producing different outcomes according to human consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bellarmine’s distinction between congruism and Molinism
rubrics_metrics.description: Bellarmine distinguishes his view (close to Augustinian) from extreme Molinism: both assign internal suasion in the aid, but differ on whether efficaciousness depends on human will or on God’s will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bellarmine’s treatment shows an attempt to preserve Augustinian/Tridentine emphases while addressing Molinist objections; used as an interpretive key for comparing positions on efficacy and human cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocatio efficax (effective calling) defined by congruity
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Vocatio efficax’ is that which includes a certain congruity with respect to the person so that it is proportionate and adapted to produce the effect infallibly in that person, at that time and circumstance (Suarez).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in debates to argue that some divine calls are ‘efficient’ because God orders circumstances and aids so that effect follows; contrasted with views that make efficacy depend solely on foreseen human consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction and ranking of theological schools (Thomism, Augustinianism, Molinism, Congruism, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text catalogues main schools (Calvinism, Bajanism, Jansenism—Thomism, Augustinianism, Molinism, and Congruism) and attributes characteristic claims regarding grace and freedom to each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as an evaluative taxonomy: understanding a doctrine requires situating it within these schools and their characteristic claims about efficacious/prevenient grace, foreknowledge, and merits; numerous citations provide exemplars and critiques for each school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural and patristic proofs for doctrines of grace and predestination
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of scriptural passages (e.g., Rom. VIII, 29; Matth. XXV, 34; John VI; Rom. IX, 19; Heb. XI, 6) and patristic citations to ground positions on predestination, vocation, and faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats Scripture and Fathers as primary warrants for doctrinal formulations; interpretive moves (e.g., Augustine, Chrysostom) are marshaled for and against positions such as election from foreknowledge, necessity of faith, and the character of divine calling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even efficacious grace can be rejected (Tridentine nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement citing Tridentine material: a man receiving that inspiration (gratiam efficacem) may receive it and yet cast it off (‘illam et abiicere potest’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects the delicate balance in Tridentine and post-Tridentine theology avoiding formulations that make efficacious grace either irresistible in the simple sense or denying real human responsibility; the exact sense is debated and contextualized with other canons that also assert God’s effective motion.
